raw_evidence.label: Most geographically spread Winter Games ever
raw_evidence.content: Milano Cortina 2026 was the most geographically widespread Winter Olympic Games in history, with venues sprawled across more than 22,000 square kilometres of northern Italy. The schedule moved athletes and spectators across a 530-mile arc connecting Milan (ice sports), Bormio (men's alpine + ski mountaineering), Livigno (snowboard, freestyle), Cortina d'Ampezzo (women's alpine, sliding, curling), Predazzo and Tesero in Val di Fiemme (ski jumping, cross-country, Nordic combined), Anterselva in South Tyrol (biathlon), and Verona (closing ceremony). A full circuit of mountain venues required nearly 13 hours of non-stop driving — a fact baked into how 'spread thin' the daily schedule looks in the data: 14 distinct venues hosting 1,866 sessions over 19 days.

raw_evidence.label: Cortina hosts the most sessions; Anterselva is 100% medal
raw_evidence.content: Cortina d'Ampezzo hosts the largest cluster of sessions (757 across three venues — curling, sliding centre, and Tofane alpine), partly because the curling stadium alone runs 436 round-robin sessions. The most extreme cluster is the Anterselva Biathlon Arena: 33 sessions, 33 medal events — 100% medal density, because biathlon's training does not appear on the public schedule. Bormio, host to alpine men's events and ski mountaineering, runs 53 sessions of which 24 (45%) are medal events — the highest competition-only density of any single venue.

raw_evidence.label: NBC's 23.5M average; viewership doubles vs Beijing
raw_evidence.content: Milano Cortina 2026 became the highest-rated Winter Games on US television since Sochi 2014, averaging 23.5 million viewers across NBC, Peacock, CNBC and USA Network — up 96% from Beijing 2022. The Saturday primetime slot peaked at 28.5 million combined viewers. The men's hockey final pulled 20.7 million — the biggest hockey audience since the 2010 gold-medal game — while the US-Canada women's hockey gold final drew a record-breaking 5.3 million. These numbers matter for the dataset because they hint at which prime-time evening sessions the schedule was engineered around: ice hockey medal games and figure skating finals tend to dominate the late-evening Italian local time slots that align with US prime time.

raw_evidence.label: Time zone math for prime-time scheduling
raw_evidence.content: Italy is on Central European Time (UTC+1) in February. US Eastern Time runs UTC-5, so an event starting at 19:00 local Italian time begins at 13:00 ET — perfect for NBC's 'prime afternoon' window. A 21:00 Italian start hits 15:00 ET, just before East Coast evening prime time. China and East Asia (UTC+8) are 7 hours ahead of Italy, meaning an Italian morning session lands in Chinese late afternoon. This affects the dataset's start_time distribution: high-profile medal events skew to mid-evening Italian time, while pool play and training fill morning slots. The schedule's start-hour histogram should reveal a bimodal pattern — late mornings for training, evenings for medals — and the medal-event subset will hug 17:00–21:00 local.

raw_evidence.content: Start times concentrate in two clear bands. The 14:00 local slot is the largest single hour with 305 sessions (16% of the entire schedule), driven by curling round-robins, sliding heats, and afternoon snow events. medal_df = df[df['is_medal_event']==True].copy()

morning = medal_df[(medal_df['hour']<10)]
print(f"Medal events 18:00-21:59 local (= afternoon US ET): {len(prime_window)} ({len(prime_window)/len(medal_df)*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"Medal events 10:00-12:59 local (= dawn US ET): {len(afternoon)} ({len(afternoon)/len(medal_df)*100:.1f}%)")

The schedule moved athletes and spectators across a 530-mile arc connecting Milan (ice sports), Bormio (men's alpine + ski mountaineering), Livigno (snowboard, freestyle), Cortina d'Ampezzo (women's alpine, sliding, curling), Predazzo and Tesero in Val di Fiemme (ski jumping, cross-country, Nordic combined), Anterselva in South Tyrol (biathlon), and Verona (closing ceremony). Cortina hosts 55 medal sessions, dominated by sliding sports — luge 15, alpine 12, bobsleigh 11, skeleton 9, curling 8. raw_evidence.label: Curling's session-count outlier
raw_evidence.content: Curling occupies a uniquely large slice of the schedule — 436 sessions in the dataset, more than any other sport — because its pool play and round-robin format requires every team to play every other team across both men's, women's, and mixed doubles disciplines. Each session is also long (2+ hours). This is a known quirk: curling has only 8 medal events but consumes hundreds of session slots. Designers should treat the curling spike as a structural feature of the data, not a story angle on its own. Conversely, sports like ski mountaineering (only 21 sessions, but 9 medal events relative to that low total) have a much higher 'medal density' per session.
